headline: P0064 (Family Practice, GA): 99215 share of 28.8% against 3.5% expected for its patient mix, elevated at every complexity tier including patients with 0-1 chronic conditions
rationale: The provider billed 72 of 250 claims (28.8%) as 99215, against an expected share of about 3.5% given patient complexity (z vs peers 3.58, risk-adjusted score 7.96). The panel does not look unusually sick: 124 of 250 visits are for patients with 0-1 chronic conditions, and only 1 visit is for a patient with 5+ conditions. The excess holds at every complexity tier. On low-complexity patients the provider's 99215 share is 15.2% vs 2.1% for all providers (0 conditions) and 19.2% vs 3.4% (1 condition). Sampled low-complexity 99215s include single-symptom visits coded only as rash R21 (C0028395, C0028417, C0028459, C0028627), low back pain (C0028513), upper respiratory infection (C0028577) and abdominal pain (C0028531). There are also repeat 99215s for one stable chronic condition, such as hyperlipidemia (C0028397, C0028451) and hypertension (C0028562, C0028566). 99214 also makes up most of the billing (133 claims), including a sampled rash-only visit (C0028435). 99215s on 4-condition patients (e.g., C0028495, C0028583) are more plausible, although the provider's share there (48%) is still well above peers (13.9%). Taken together, this is consistent with upcoding rather than a high-acuity panel. The claim lists are random samples, and no clinical documentation, time records or MDM support is in the packet, so the pattern is not confirmed.
next_steps: Request medical records for the sampled low-complexity 99215 claims (e.g., C0028395, C0028417, C0028459, C0028627, C0028577) and check MDM level or documented total time against 2021+ E/M guidelines.
Review repeat 99215 visits for the same patient with one stable condition (P0064-N0038, P0064-N0061, P0064-N0009, P0064-N0081) for medical necessity and changes in clinical status.
Pull a statistically valid random sample of all 99214/99215 claims for coding review to estimate an error rate before drawing any conclusions about the whole population.
Check whether time-based coding, templated notes or EHR auto-leveling are driving levels, and whether add-on or prolonged-service codes appear.
Compare against the provider's prior-period billing mix and confirm the risk-adjustment inputs (chronic condition counts) are complete, in case diagnoses are under-captured.
